# The problem

## AI coding assistants want CLI tools

- `git`, `gcloud`, `kubectl`, `npm`, `terraform`, ...
- They are essential for real productivity.
- Giving them direct shell access means handing over **every secret
  on the machine**.

::: {.fragment}
> "Just run `gcloud` for me." → the model now sees your service
> account key file path, and every command it issues runs as you.
:::

## Threats in scope

The **whole workspace is untrusted** — the assistant, its tool calls,
*and* the build/test/dependency code they trigger.

- Goal-directed model behaviour (intentional probing).
- Prompt-injection into long-running sessions.
- Output exfiltration via stdout / stderr.
- Shell-metacharacter injection in command arguments.
- Supply-chain compromise — a malicious `postinstall` or a poisoned
  transitive dep pulled in during a routine dependency update —
  bounded by the throwaway `wraptool up` container.

::: {.fragment}
Honest scope: the container isolates **host credentials** and bounds
ops by the whitelist. It still has network + the source tree and shares
the agent's policed MCP tools — so it does **not** guarantee source
confidentiality or block egress.
:::

## What we want

| Want | Today |
|------|-------|
| Allow `git commit` | ✅ shell access |
| Deny `git push --force` | ❌ shell access |
| Audit every command | ❌ shell access |
| Never see `~/.ssh/id_*` | ❌ shell access |
| Rotate credentials independently | ❌ shell access |

---

# The idea

## A tiny MCP gateway in front of the CLI

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  ai[AI assistant] -- MCP --> wt[wraptool] --> cli[CLI binary]
  wt --- creds[(creds)]
  style creds fill:#fee,stroke:#E60028
```

- wraptool is an **MCP server**: every harness already knows how to
  talk to one.
- It runs as a **separate process** with its own environment.
- It enforces a **per-tool, per-subcommand, per-flag** whitelist.

## Why not just `sudo` rules / SELinux / AppArmor?

- Those constrain the **process tree**, not the **call**.
- They cannot see "`git push --force`" as a structured object — only
  bytes through exec.
- They cannot send a structured denial back to the AI.
- They cannot turn `--help` output into an MCP tool schema.

# Architecture

## One process per trust domain

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  subgraph untrusted ["Untrusted: AI sandbox"]
    ai["AI + harness"]
  end
  subgraph trusted ["Trusted: host"]
    wt["wraptool"]
    creds[("SSH / gcloud / kube")]
    bins["/usr/bin/git, ..."]
  end
  ai <-- "SSE / Unix sock" --> wt
  wt --- creds
  wt --> bins
  style untrusted fill:#fee,stroke:#E60028
  style trusted fill:#efe,stroke:#2a7
```

## The sandbox is a real container

`wraptool up` (or bare `wraptool` in a repo) backs the "untrusted"
box with an actual throwaway container:

- **Guix-native** — `guix shell --container --network --emulate-fhs
  -m manifest.scm` when `guix` is present, else a **Dev Container**.
- **user + mount namespace** — host `$HOME` and secrets are **never**
  mounted; local git works in-box, privileged git still goes through
  the MCP tool.
- Same flat toolchain as the developer's, so the harness can
  compile / test / analyze locally.
- Harness installed + wired, host gateway auto-detected.

## Inside wraptool

```
main.go
cmd/      up · down · server · harness · validate
          init (+ init devcontainer) · serve · requests · root
internal/
  config/         YAML types + Validate + ApplyRequest
  whitelist/      deny > allow > flag / arg constraints
  executor/       exec.CommandContext, sanitization, scrubbing
  mcptools/       MCP tool registry, handler, request_capability
  introspect/     --help parsing (git / GNU / fallback), cache
  requestlog/     JSONL store
  webui/          operator request-review Web UI
  harness/        harness descriptor registry
  paths/          XDG via adrg/xdg
```

## Evaluation flow

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart LR
  call([Tool call]) --> tool{Tool<br/>configured?}
  tool -- yes --> deny{Deny<br/>match?}
  deny -- no --> allow{Allow<br/>match?}
  allow -- yes --> flags{Flags +<br/>constraints?}
  flags -- yes --> args{Args<br/>ok?}
  args -- yes --> exec([Execute])

  tool  -- no  --> X([Refuse])
  deny  -- yes --> X
  allow -- no  --> X
  flags -- no  --> X
  args  -- no  --> X

  classDef ok fill:#efe,stroke:#2a7
  classDef no fill:#fee,stroke:#E60028
  class exec ok
  class X no
```

# Config

## Whitelist by example

```{.yaml code-line-numbers="|4|6|8|10|12-13|15"}
tools:
  git:
    binary: /usr/bin/git
    timeout: 30s
    allow:
      - subcommand: [status]
        flags: ["--short", "--branch", "--porcelain"]
      - subcommand: [commit]
        flags: ["--message", "--amend"]
        flag_constraints:
          "--message": { required: true }
      - subcommand: [push]
        flags: ["--set-upstream"]
        deny_flags: ["--force", "--force-with-lease"]
    deny:
      - subcommand: [remote, set-url]
```

## Auto-discovery

- wraptool runs `<tool> --help` at startup.
- Parses git-style, GNU-style, fallback regex.
- Generates MCP tool schemas with **real descriptions**, **types**,
  **required flags**.
- Cache in `~/.cache/wraptool/introspection/`.
- YAML overrides for the inevitable misparses.

# Security in depth

## What the AI never sees

- The wraptool config.
- Any environment variable except those a tool's own output prints.
- Anything that looks like a credential (Bearer tokens, AWS keys,
  SSH key markers, configured env values — all scrubbed).
- Stdout/stderr beyond 1 MB per call.

## What we kill at the door

- `sh -c` — **never used**. Always `exec.CommandContext` with an
  explicit argv.
- Shell metacharacters in positional args: `;|&$\`(){}` rejected.
- Args starting with `-` in positional slots: rejected.
- Long-running processes: per-tool `context.WithTimeout`.

## Network transports

- `sse`, `unix`.
- The HTTP listener serves **both** legacy SSE at `/sse` **and**
  Streamable HTTP at `/mcp` behind one Bearer wrapper (Antigravity
  negotiates the latter).
- `sse` + `unix` support `auth_token_file` with constant-time bearer
  comparison.
- Unix socket auto-`chmod 0600`.

# Operations

## Hot-reload

- File watcher (`fsnotify`) on the **parent directory**, 200 ms
  debounce.
- SIGHUP still works (scripts, containers without inotify).
- Atomic policy swap; in-flight commands keep the old policy.
- `notifications/tools/list_changed` pushed to every connected client.

## Capability requests

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
  AI ->> wraptool: denied call
  wraptool -->> AI: structured refusal + hint
  AI ->> wraptool: wraptool_request_capability(...)
  wraptool ->> log: append (pending)
  Operator ->> log: requests list
  Operator ->> wraptool: requests approve --apply
  wraptool ->> config: ApplyRequest (atomic)
  config -->> wraptool: fsnotify event
  wraptool -->> AI: list_changed
```

## `approve --apply`

- Edits the YAML **node tree** (`yaml.v3`), so **comments and
  ordering are preserved**.
- Refuses unknown tools (no `binary`) and deny-rule conflicts.
- Validates the result before atomic rename into place.
- File-watch reload picks it up — no restart, no client reconnect.

# Demo

## Live walkthrough

::: {.incremental}
1. `wraptool up` (or bare `wraptool`) in a repo → **one command**
   brings up a credential-isolated container with the harness
   installed and wired, host gateway auto-detected.
   - Guix-native container from `manifest.scm` if `guix` is present,
     else a Dev Container.
2. Allowed: `git_status`, `git_commit_message="..."`.
3. Denied: `git_push --force` → structured refusal.
4. AI calls `wraptool_request_capability` with rationale.
5. Operator: `wraptool requests list`, then
   `wraptool requests approve req_xxxx --apply`.
6. fsnotify → reload → new tool registered → AI's next call
   succeeds. **No restart.**
:::

::: {.fragment}
Minimal, no-container fallback: `wraptool init --harness claude`
to wire a harness at any MCP client, then `wraptool server start` on the host.
:::

# Where next

## Roadmap

- Per-tool output filters (jq-style projection before scrub).
- Per-session quotas (calls/minute, bytes out).
- Pluggable scrubbers for org-specific secret formats.
- A "dry-run" mode that records what *would* be denied.
